practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Witan in Anglo-Saxon England.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific feature (e.g. advised the king on major decisions) AND develops it with accurate supporting detail (e.g. played a key role in choosing Harold Godwinson as king in January 1066). Secure: identifies a valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague or partially accurate feature. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the thegn class in Anglo-Saxon England.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: clear identification of a specific feature with precise supporting detail for each (e.g. thegns provided military service — typically one warrior per five hides of land; thegns administered local justice in the shire courts). Secure: both features identified with some development. Developing: one feature fully developed, one vague. Emerging: one vague feature or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the king's peace was important to Anglo-Saxon government.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more well-developed reasons with specific supporting detail and a clear explanation of how each reason mattered (e.g. the king's peace defined crimes against travellers or at royal locations as personal affronts to the king, allowing heavier penalties and reinforcing the idea that royal authority extended across the whole kingdom; law codes like those of Æthelred II formalised these principles and gave thegns the framework to enforce them locally). Secure: two reasons identified and explained with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two reasons without clear explanation of significance. Emerging: descriptive narrative with little analytical content.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Danegeld is significant evidence for the strength of Anglo-Saxon government.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies the Danegeld as a nationwide tax levy, explains how it demonstrates administrative reach (ability to assess and collect tax across all shires), links this to broader evidence of strong government (Domesday survey relied on Anglo-Saxon administrative units), and considers limitations (military failure despite this capacity). Secure: explains significance with specific detail but analysis of limitations is partial. Developing: describes the Danegeld accurately but treats it only as evidence of Viking pressure rather than of administrative capacity. Emerging: vague reference to Viking tribute without engagement with the question.

practice_questions.text: How far did the Witan limit the power of Anglo-Saxon kings? Use your knowledge of the period to support your answer. [You may consider: the role of the Witan in succession decisions; the relationship between kings and the thegn class; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument that assesses the extent of Witan constraint across the whole period c.1000-1066, with precise evidence (Harold Godwinson's selection, Cnut's use of the Witan, Edward the Confessor's piety limiting his authority); considers counterargument (kings still led armies, issued law codes, held ultimate military command); reaches an overall judgement. Secure: clear argument addressing both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance between periods or factors. Developing: describes Witan role accurately but does not weigh it against royal power; limited range of evidence. Emerging: narrative account of Anglo-Saxon kingship without addressing the question of extent.

practice_questions.text: Outline the key features of royal power in Anglo-Saxon England c.1000-1066.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more accurate, specific points about features of royal power (e.g. hereditary right via House of Wessex; Church-sanctioned coronation; Witan as advisory council; thegns as local agents; king's peace as legal framework; Danegeld as national tax). Secure: two or three relevant features with some supporting detail. Developing: one or two features with limited accuracy or detail. Emerging: vague reference to kings having power with no specific features.

before.exam_tip_html: When answering “Explain Why” questions on Anglo-Saxon kingship, avoid simply listing features of the Witan or the thegn class. Each reason needs a clear chain: identify the factor, explain how it affected royal power specifically, then show what changed or what consequence followed. Examiners reward a three-stage explanation — identification, specific detail, and significance — not a list of features dressed as reasons.

lessons.title: The Norman monarchy and feudal power 1066-1154

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the feudal system introduced by William I after 1066.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific feature (e.g. all land was technically owned by the king) AND develops it with accurate supporting detail (e.g. tenants-in-chief held land from the king and provided knights in return, creating a chain of military obligation). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague or partially accurate feature. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Domesday Book.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific supporting detail (e.g. it surveyed who held land before and after the Conquest — commissioners questioned local juries in every county; it was used as a basis for taxation — William needed to know what his kingdom was worth). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: one vague feature or irrelevant content.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Oath of Salisbury was significant for the development of royal power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more well-developed reasons with specific evidence (the Oath of 1086 required all landowners to swear loyalty directly to William, bypassing their immediate lords — this overrode the feudal logic of competing loyalties; it established a principle that the king's claim was supreme across the entire kingdom, unlike the advisory role of the Anglo-Saxon Witan). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped reasons. Emerging: descriptive account of Norman rule without addressing significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain why baronial support was essential to Norman kings despite their feudal power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains the paradox — the feudal system gave kings ultimate authority over land but kings still needed barons to govern, administer justice and defend the kingdom; uses specific evidence (William I's kingdom split after his death as barons chose sides; Henry I had to issue the Charter of Liberties to secure support; the Anarchy 1135-54 showed what happened when baronial loyalty was divided). Secure: explains the tension with relevant evidence but analysis is partial. Developing: describes baronial power accurately but does not explain why it constrained kings. Emerging: vague points about barons being powerful.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Norman Conquest in changing the power of the monarchy? Use your knowledge of the period c.1000-1154 to support your answer. [You may consider: the feudal system; the Domesday Book; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument addressing both change (feudal land tenure, Domesday, Oath of Salisbury — far tighter royal control than Anglo-Saxon Witan model) and continuity (kings still needed baronial support; succession remained contested; Charter of Liberties suggests limits on power were accepted); precise evidence across 1066-1154; clear overall judgement on the degree of change. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes Norman changes accurately but treats them as uniformly strengthening royal power without considering limits. Emerging: narrative of the Conquest without addressing the question of significance.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main ways William I extended royal power in England after 1066.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points (feudal land tenure from the king; replacement of English landowners with Normans; Domesday survey as a tax and administrative tool; Oath of Salisbury 1086; Harrying of the North to crush rebellion). Secure: two or three relevant points with supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to William being powerful.

before.exam_tip_html: The Domesday Book appears frequently in questions about Norman royal power. When you use it as evidence, remember to treat it as a historian would — note what it shows (administrative reach, the scale of the Norman takeover) but also its limitations as a source (no London, no Winchester, omits the far north, primarily a tax record). Examiners reward students who handle sources critically rather than as simple facts to quote.
before.content_html:
The Conquest and Transfer of Power

On 14 October 1066 William of Normandy defeated Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Hastings. Harold was killed — most accounts suggest he died late in the battle — and within weeks the remaining English leaders submitted to William. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066. The speed of submission masked how total the transfer of power really was: within twenty years, almost every major English landowner had been replaced by a Norman.

William’s conquest was not just a change of king. It was a wholesale replacement of the ruling class. The feudal system William introduced tied land ownership directly to military service, creating a new chain of obligation that ran from the king at the top through his tenants-in-chief down to ordinary knights and peasants.

Key Fact

Under William I, all land in England was technically owned by the king. He granted it to tenants-in-chief (his great barons) who provided knights in return. This made every landowner ultimately dependent on royal favour — a far tighter grip on power than the Anglo-Saxon Witan had allowed.

Domesday Book 1086

In 1085–86, William ordered a comprehensive survey of England to find out who held what land and what it was worth in tax. The result was the Domesday Book. Commissioners travelled to every county, questioning local juries about the land: who held it before the Conquest (“in the time of King Edward”), who held it now, how many people lived there, and what it was worth.

The Domesday Book is a remarkable piece of evidence, but historians use it with care. It covers most of England but omits London, Winchester and much of the far north. It is primarily a tax record, not a population census, and it underrepresents the poorest people. Nevertheless, it demonstrates the administrative ambition of Norman kingship — a king who could survey an entire kingdom in a year wielded far greater state power than most medieval rulers.

William’s grip was not established without violence. When northern English lords and Danish allies rebelled in 1069, William responded with systematic destruction of crops, livestock and settlements across Yorkshire and the surrounding counties — an event later called the Harrying of the North. Contemporary chronicler Orderic Vitalis described vast areas left depopulated. Domesday entries for parts of Yorkshire still record villages as “waste” over fifteen years later.

The Harrying was deliberate — William intended to destroy the economic base of rebellion. It is evidence that Norman power in the north was achieved through terror as well as feudal structures. However, historians debate its true scale: Domesday’s “waste” entries may reflect tax classification rather than physical destruction throughout.

The Extent of Royal Power by 1087

By the time William I died in 1087 he had transformed the relationship between king and barons. The Oath of Salisbury of 1086 required every significant landowner in England to swear direct loyalty to the king, regardless of who their immediate lord was. This cut across the feudal logic that a man’s first loyalty was to the lord directly above him, and gave William a personal claim on every landholder in the country.

Yet William also needed his barons. Without them he could not govern, administer justice, or defend the kingdom. When he died, the kingdom immediately fractured: his son William II took England while another son, Robert Curthose, took Normandy. Baronial support for each claimant was crucial. This tension — between a king’s need for baronial cooperation and his desire to limit baronial independence — would define English politics for the next century.

Key Fact

The Oath of Salisbury (1086) made all English landowners swear loyalty directly to William I, bypassing their immediate lords. This was a significant extension of royal authority — it meant the king’s claim superseded all other loyalties in the feudal chain.

Henry I (king 1100–1135) came to power after his brother William II’s sudden death in a hunting accident. To secure baronial support, he issued a Charter of Liberties (1100), promising to end certain abuses of royal power and to respect the rights of the Church and barons. Though Henry often broke these promises in practice, the Charter established an important principle: a king could be expected to govern within agreed limits. Historians have noted its influence on Magna Carta 115 years later.

Henry’s reign also showed the continuing fragility of succession. When his son drowned in the White Ship disaster of 1120, Henry tried to secure his daughter Empress Matilda as successor. After Henry’s death in 1135, the barons backed his nephew Stephen instead, leading to a period of civil conflict known as “the Anarchy” (1135–54) and demonstrating once more that baronial consent was essential to effective kingship.

lessons.title: Magna Carta and the emergence of Parliament 1199-1399

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Magna Carta (1215).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific clause or principle (e.g. Clause 39 established that no free man could be imprisoned without lawful judgement) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. this was a direct response to John's arbitrary use of royal courts to punish barons who opposed him). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to 'limiting the king' without specifics. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the parliament called by Simon de Montfort in 1265.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. it included knights from each county — the first parliament to represent ordinary landowners below the baronial class; it included burgesses from towns — bringing in representatives of the trading community for the first time). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: one vague feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the barons rebelled against King John and forced him to seal Magna Carta in 1215.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more well-developed reasons with specific evidence (loss of Normandy 1204 damaged baronial French estates and reflected military failure John blamed on barons; John raised taxation beyond feudal custom to fund his wars, demanding payments the barons saw as illegal; John manipulated royal courts and took noble hostages, violating accepted norms of justice — Clause 39 directly addressed this). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped ones. Emerging: narrative of John being unpopular without analytical reasons.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the development of Parliament in the thirteenth century was significant for the future of royal power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains how each step was significant for later constitutional development (Magna Carta established the principle of legal limits on kingship — reissued multiple times, it became a constitutional reference point; de Montfort's 1265 parliament established that governance could include non-noble representatives; Edward I's Model Parliament 1295 made representative taxation consent a regular practice — setting a precedent monarchs later struggled to reverse). Secure: two steps explained with specific evidence. Developing: describes parliamentary development accurately but does not explain why each step mattered. Emerging: vague points about Parliament becoming more powerful.

practice_questions.text: How far did Magna Carta and the growth of Parliament change the relationship between the monarchy and its subjects in the period 1199-1399? [You may consider: Magna Carta 1215; the parliaments of 1265 and 1295; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument weighing change against continuity — change: Magna Carta limited arbitrary royal power in principle; de Montfort's 1265 parliament included commoners; Model Parliament established taxation by consent; Richard II's deposition 1399 showed parliament could be used to remove a monarch. Continuity: kings still dominated; John rejected Magna Carta immediately; de Montfort was crushed; Parliament met at royal summons only; Wars of the Roses showed military power still trumped constitutional principles. Overall judgement required. Secure: both sides argued with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes the growth of Parliament without weighing change vs continuity. Emerging: narrative account without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the key events in the emergence of Parliament between 1215 and 1295.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points in sequence (Magna Carta 1215 — barons force limits on John; Provisions of Oxford 1258 — baronial council imposed on Henry III; de Montfort's parliament 1265 — first with knights and burgesses; Model Parliament 1295 — Edward I formalises representative assembly for taxation). Secure: two or three relevant points with some supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to Parliament developing.

before.exam_tip_html: Examiner reports for this thematic unit repeatedly flag the confusion between King John and Charles I. Remember: John’s dispute with the barons was about feudal taxation and the abuse of royal courts (1215). Charles I’s dispute was about ship money and religious policy (1629-42). Magna Carta belongs to John; the Petition of Right and the Civil War belong to Charles. Getting the monarch wrong can cost marks even when the surrounding argument is correct.
before.content_html:
John and the Road to Magna Carta

King John (reigned 1199–1216) inherited a kingdom already strained by his brother Richard I’s costly crusading and ransom payments. John then lost his French lands — including the valuable Duchy of Normandy in 1204 — to the French crown. To finance his attempts to win them back, John raised taxes repeatedly and used royal prerogative in ways the barons found intolerable: demanding feudal payments beyond custom, taking hostages, and manipulating the royal courts.

The barons’ grievances centred on taxation and the arbitrary use of royal power. Note carefully: their dispute with John was about taxation without consent and the abuse of royal courts, not about ship money (which is Charles I, 400 years later) or religious policy (which is a Tudor issue). Keeping these rulers distinct is essential.

Key Fact

The barons’ grievances against John were specific: excessive taxation beyond feudal custom, the taking of noble hostages, manipulation of royal courts to deny justice, and the loss of Normandy which damaged baronial estates in France. These drove the rebellion that produced Magna Carta in 1215.

Magna Carta 1215

In June 1215, after a baronial army seized London, John met the barons at Runnymede and sealed the Magna Carta. The document covered 63 clauses. Most dealt with specific feudal grievances, but three clauses had lasting constitutional significance:

  • Clause 39: no free man shall be imprisoned or stripped of rights “except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land.”
  • Clause 40: “To no one will we sell, to no one will we deny or delay right or justice.”
  • Clause 12: taxation beyond feudal custom required the “common counsel of the realm.”

John immediately sought papal annulment of the Charter, which Innocent III granted in August 1215. Civil war resumed. John died in October 1216 and Magna Carta was reissued by his young successor Henry III’s regents to secure support. It was confirmed multiple times in the thirteenth century and became a touchstone for later generations arguing that royal power had legal limits.

Henry III’s long reign (1216–1272) was marked by repeated conflicts with his barons over royal favourites and taxation. In 1258 the barons forced Henry to accept the Provisions of Oxford, creating a permanent baronial council to oversee royal government. Henry rejected the Provisions in 1261, leading to the Second Barons’ War (1264–65).

The rebel leader was Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester. After defeating Henry III at the Battle of Lewes in 1264, de Montfort called a parliament in January 1265 that, for the first time, included not just barons and bishops but also knights from each county and burgesses (representatives) from some towns. This “parliament of commoners” was a revolutionary step — governance was no longer just a matter for the great magnates.

De Montfort was killed at the Battle of Evesham in August 1265 and his rebellion was crushed. But the idea that representatives of ordinary freemen should be consulted in government did not die with him.

Edward I and the Model Parliament

Edward I (reigned 1272–1307) needed money for his wars in Wales, Scotland and France. He developed the practice of calling regular parliaments to grant taxation — and by 1295 he called what later became known as the Model Parliament. It included not just bishops and barons but also two knights from each county and two burgesses from each major town.

The Model Parliament was not a democratic institution. Representatives were summoned because the king needed their agreement to tax, not because he wished to share power. Edward’s famous principle — “what touches all should be approved by all” — was practical, not idealistic. Yet by establishing that taxation required consent from a representative body, Edward was building a constitutional convention that would become increasingly important over the next four centuries.

Key Fact

The Model Parliament of 1295 included two knights from each county and two burgesses from each major town, alongside bishops and barons. This mix of clergy, nobility and commons is the model for the later English Parliament of Lords and Commons.

Richard II (reigned 1377–1399) tried to assert royal authority in absolute terms, dismissing magnates and manipulating Parliament. In 1399 a coalition of barons and clergy forced his deposition and replaced him with Henry Bolingbroke (Henry IV). Parliament formally approved the deposition — making the constitutional point that kingship could be conditional on good governance.

The subsequent Wars of the Roses (1455–1487) were a dynastic conflict between the Lancastrian and Yorkist branches of the royal family. They weakened the baronial class through battle casualties and attainders, creating the conditions in which Tudor monarchs could later centralise power more effectively. Parliament existed throughout this period, though it largely deferred to whichever king was militarily dominant.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Henry VIII used Parliament to achieve the English Reformation rather than acting through royal decree alone.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (statute law was harder to reverse than royal decree — giving the Reformation permanence; Parliamentary approval gave the break with Rome legal force that could be used to punish opposition through treason charges; Cromwell's management of Parliament made it an effective legislative tool; routing the Reformation through Parliament also confirmed Parliament's role in major constitutional changes — a double-edged consequence). practice_questions.text: Explain why Elizabeth I's management of Parliament faced growing challenges by the 1590s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains two or more factors with specific evidence (the 'Puritan choir' of MPs persistently introduced Church reform bills Elizabeth regarded as infringing on royal prerogative, which she had to veto repeatedly; the monopolies dispute of 1601 led to Elizabeth's Golden Speech conceding that her advisers had misinformed her — a rare public admission; the succession question never resolved, creating anxiety among MPs that a Catholic heir could undo the Protestant settlement). practice_questions.text: How far did the Reformation increase the power of Parliament in Tudor England? [You may consider: the Reformation Parliament; Elizabeth I's management of Parliament; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument with evidence from across the Tudor period — change: Reformation Parliament legislated on the most fundamental questions of Church and state; dissolution of monasteries created a gentry class with stake in Protestant Parliament; Parliament's legislative role grew in sophistication under Cromwell's management; Elizabeth had to use prerogative carefully and concede on monopolies. Continuity: monarchs still controlled when Parliament met; Elizabeth successfully blocked Church reform bills; Parliament met only when summoned. Overall judgement required. Secure: argues both sides with specific evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes Parliamentary role accurately but does not weigh increase in power against continuities. Emerging: narrative of Tudor history without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main ways Henry VIII used Parliament to carry out the English Reformation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points (Reformation Parliament 1529-36 passed a series of Acts cutting ties with Rome; Act of Supremacy 1534 made Henry Supreme Head of the Church; Cromwell managed the parliamentary programme; dissolution of the monasteries 1536-40 carried out by statute; Treasons Act 1534 made denial of supremacy capital). Secure: two or three relevant points with some detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to Henry using Parliament.

before.content_html:
Tudor Government and the Use of Parliament

The Tudor monarchs — Henry VII (1485–1509), Henry VIII (1509–1547), Edward VI (1547–1553), Mary I (1553–1558) and Elizabeth I (1558–1603) — inherited a kingdom whose barons had been weakened by the Wars of the Roses. This gave them an opportunity to centralise royal power. Yet the Tudor story is not simply one of growing royal authority. Parliament’s role in the Reformation meant that it became more powerful, not less, as the sixteenth century progressed.

Henry VIII used Parliament to give his break with Rome a legal foundation that no subsequent monarch could easily reverse. This was both brilliant and double-edged: by routing the Reformation through statute, Henry made Parliament the instrument of royal policy — but he also confirmed that fundamental constitutional changes required parliamentary approval.

Key Fact

The Reformation Parliament sat from 1529 to 1536 and passed a series of Acts that severed England from Rome: culminating in the Act of Supremacy (1534), which made Henry VIII the “Supreme Head of the Church of England.” No pope, no foreign religious authority, had any power in England.

The Reformation Parliament and the Act of Supremacy

Henry VIII’s desire for an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon — and the Pope’s refusal to grant it — created the context for the English Reformation. His chief minister Thomas Cromwell designed a legislative programme that used Parliament to achieve what the Pope would not grant. Between 1529 and 1536 a series of Acts progressively cut the ties between England and Rome.

The Act of Supremacy (1534) was the centrepiece. By passing it through Parliament, Henry gave the Reformation the force of statute law, making it treasonous to deny his religious supremacy. This was parliamentary power deployed in the service of royal policy — but it also meant Parliament had legislated on the most fundamental questions of religion and authority.

Thomas Cromwell turned Parliament into an effective legislative machine. He managed elections, drafted bills, and coordinated the passage of legislation — skills that helped Parliament become a more sophisticated institution. Historians sometimes describe this as the “Tudor revolution in government”: a shift from a personal, household-based monarchy towards a bureaucratic, statute-based state.

Cromwell was executed in 1540 after arranging Henry’s disastrous fourth marriage to Anne of Cleves. But the parliamentary machinery he created outlasted him. The dissolution of the monasteries (1536–40), carried out under his direction, redistributed enormous amounts of Church land to the gentry — creating a class of landowners with a direct financial stake in the Protestant settlement and, therefore, in Parliament protecting it.

Elizabeth I and Parliament

Elizabeth I (reigned 1558–1603) was a skilled manager of Parliament rather than a dominator of it. She called Parliament 13 times in 45 years — always when she needed money or legislation — and generally got what she asked for. But she faced persistent pressure from MPs on issues she considered her royal prerogative: religion, her marriage and the succession.

The Elizabethan Settlement of 1559 reset England’s religious position after Mary I had returned it to Catholicism. Elizabeth’s settlement was deliberately broad — she wanted a church that most English people could accept. Parliament passed both the Act of Supremacy (making her Supreme Governor) and the Act of Uniformity (imposing the Book of Common Prayer), giving the settlement statutory force.

Key Fact

Elizabeth I took the title “Supreme Governor” of the Church of England rather than “Supreme Head” (Henry VIII’s title). This was a deliberate softening designed to be more acceptable to Catholics and to the Church hierarchy who objected to a woman being called “head” of the Church.

Despite her parliamentary skill, Elizabeth faced MPs who pushed for more Protestant reform than she wanted. The “Puritan choir” of MPs regularly introduced bills on Church discipline that Elizabeth regarded as intruding on royal prerogative. She used her veto to block them, but could not stop MPs raising them.

The succession question was the most persistent tension. MPs repeatedly urged Elizabeth to marry and name an heir, fearing a Catholic succession if she died childless. Elizabeth resisted these pressures throughout her reign. In her famous “Golden Speech” of 1601 she acknowledged parliamentary concerns over monopolies — licences she had granted to courtiers that MPs considered a tax on trade — conceding that she had not been well informed by her advisers. Her willingness to make this concession showed both her political skill and the increasing confidence of the Commons.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Charles I's Personal Rule (1629-1640).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific feature (e.g. Charles I levied ship money without parliamentary consent) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. originally a coastal tax, he extended it to inland counties in 1635; when John Hampden refused payment in 1637, the resulting court case attracted national attention and damaged Charles's image). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to Charles governing without Parliament. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Long Parliament's actions against royal power in 1640-41.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. the Long Parliament abolished ship money — removing Charles's main non-parliamentary revenue source; the Triennial Act 1641 required Parliament to meet at least every three years — making it impossible for any future monarch to rule without Parliament for an extended period). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: one vague feature or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Charles I's attempt to arrest five Members of Parliament in January 1642 made civil war more likely.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (it was a constitutional outrage — using force against Parliament's members undermined the claim that Charles respected the rule of law; it failed — the MPs had been warned and escaped, humiliating the king; it confirmed parliamentary fears that Charles could not be trusted to keep agreements, making compromise impossible; it drove moderate MPs who had previously supported Charles into Parliament's camp, leaving him with a smaller royalist faction). practice_questions.text: Explain why the execution of Charles I in 1649 was a significant turning point in the development of royal power.

before.content_html:
James II and the Crisis of 1688

Charles II (restored 1660) was a pragmatic ruler who avoided a direct collision with Parliament. His brother James II (king 1685–1688) was not. James was openly Catholic and determined to use royal prerogative to promote Catholic interests: he suspended the penal laws against Catholics and Dissenters using his Dispensing Power, placed Catholics in military command posts, and in June 1688 ordered the Church of England to read his Declaration of Indulgence from every pulpit. Seven bishops who refused were arrested and tried for seditious libel — but the jury acquitted them on 30 June 1688.

On the same day as the bishops’ acquittal, seven prominent Englishmen — Whig and Tory, lords and bishops — wrote to William of Orange, the Dutch Protestant stadtholder, inviting him to bring an army to England. Their letter cited James’s violations of English law and the Protestant religion. William landed at Torbay in November 1688. James’s army disintegrated, James fled to France, and Parliament declared that he had “abdicated”.

Key Fact

Three actions by James II triggered the Glorious Revolution: his use of the Dispensing Power to suspend anti-Catholic laws without Parliament; his appointment of Catholics to military commands; and his order that the Church of England read his Declaration of Indulgence from pulpits. The trial and acquittal of the Seven Bishops showed that even the judiciary would not support him.

The Bill of Rights 1689

William III and Mary II were crowned jointly in April 1689 after accepting the Bill of Rights. This was not a modern-style declaration of individual rights but a constitutional document that listed what the crown could no longer do without parliamentary consent. The Bill of Rights:

  • Banned the suspension of laws without parliamentary consent
  • Banned the maintenance of a standing army in peacetime without Parliament’s approval
  • Required free elections for MPs and free speech inside Parliament
  • Required regular Parliaments

Alongside the Bill of Rights came the Toleration Act (1689), which allowed Protestant Dissenters to worship freely. Catholics were specifically excluded from its protections, and the Act of Settlement (1701) barred Catholics from the throne entirely. The Glorious Revolution was, in this sense, a Protestant settlement — its benefits were primarily for Anglican and Dissenting Protestants, not all subjects.

The term “Glorious Revolution” was coined by Protestants who saw 1688 as a bloodless, providential deliverance from Catholic tyranny. This framing needs critical examination. James II’s flight, not a formal battle, explains the lack of English bloodshed — but William’s campaign involved real violence in Ireland (the Williamite Wars of 1689–91) where Catholic support for James was strongest.

From a Catholic or Jacobite perspective, 1688 was not glorious — it was the violent overthrow of the legitimate king by a foreign army funded by Dutch commercial interests. The Jacobite cause (support for James and his heirs) persisted for decades, culminating in the 1715 and 1745 Jacobite rebellions. Presenting 1688 in balanced terms means acknowledging these different perspectives.

Parliamentary Monarchy in the 1700s

William III needed Parliament’s money for his wars against Louis XIV of France. He called Parliament every year, and it responded by creating the Bank of England (1694) and developing the National Debt — mechanisms that gave Parliament permanent leverage over royal finances. The Triennial Act of 1694 further regularised Parliament’s role.

The death of Queen Anne without heirs led to the Act of Union with Scotland (1707) and, via the Act of Settlement, the Hanoverian succession: George I arrived in 1714 speaking little English and heavily dependent on his ministers. Under George I and George II, Robert Walpole became effectively the first Prime Minister — holding office by managing Parliament rather than through royal favour alone. By 1750 it was clear that real executive power was shifting from the king to the ministers who commanded a parliamentary majority.

Key Fact

The Bill of Rights (1689) banned the crown from: suspending laws without Parliament; maintaining a standing army in peacetime without Parliament; interfering in elections or debate in Parliament. It also required regular Parliaments. Together these constraints ended the possibility of personal rule on the Stuart model.

Robert Walpole served as First Lord of the Treasury from 1721 to 1742 — the longest continuous tenure of any British Prime Minister. He achieved this not through royal patronage alone but by managing Parliament through a network of patronage, persuasion and political organisation. His success showed that governing Britain required parliamentary skill, not just royal favour.

Walpole’s position was a product of the 1688 settlement: a monarch dependent on parliamentary taxation needed a minister who could manage Parliament. The role of “Prime Minister” was not a formal title — Walpole himself rejected it — but it described the reality that the leader of the government’s parliamentary majority now held the real executive power.

before.content_html:
The Unreformed Electoral System

By the early nineteenth century, Britain’s system of parliamentary representation had not kept pace with population change. Many rotten boroughs returned MPs despite having almost no voters: Old Sarum in Wiltshire had seven voters and two MPs; Manchester, a growing industrial city with over 100,000 people, had none. The right to vote varied chaotically between constituencies — in some a man needed a forty-shilling freehold, in others any male householder could vote. Most working-class men and all women were excluded entirely.

The economic and social pressures of industrialisation made reform increasingly urgent. A rapidly growing urban working class had no representation. The fear of popular unrest — the French Revolution was a recent memory — made many MPs nervous about ignoring pressure for change.

Key Fact

A rotten borough was a constituency with almost no voters, often controlled by a single landlord. Old Sarum (Wiltshire) had seven voters and returned two MPs. Meanwhile Manchester, with over 100,000 inhabitants, had no MP at all. This made the pre-1832 Parliament deeply unrepresentative.

The Great Reform Act 1832

The Great Reform Act of 1832 was passed by Lord Grey’s Whig government after sustained popular pressure. It abolished the worst rotten boroughs, gave seats to the new industrial towns (Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, Sheffield), and extended the vote in boroughs to men who occupied property worth at least £10 a year.

The Act nearly doubled the electorate from around 400,000 to around 650,000. But it remained a very partial reform: it said nothing about the secret ballot (votes were still cast publicly, leaving tenants vulnerable to landlord pressure), and it did not enfranchise working-class men or women. It was a reform that preserved property ownership as the qualification for political participation.

The Second Reform Act of 1867 was a much bolder step. Passed by Benjamin Disraeli’s Conservative government, it extended the vote in boroughs to male householders and some lodgers, adding around a million new voters and giving the vote to many urban working-class men for the first time. Disraeli calculated that the newly enfranchised working class would be grateful and vote Conservative — a calculation that proved partly wrong.

William Gladstone’s Third Reform Act of 1884 extended the same franchise to rural areas, adding another 1.5 million voters. The Redistribution Act of 1885 followed, redrawing constituency boundaries to reflect population. By 1885, roughly two-thirds of adult men could vote — but no women, and not the poorest urban men.

Suffragists and Suffragettes

The campaign for women’s suffrage developed two distinct wings, which students must not confuse. The suffragists — the NUWSS led by Millicent Fawcett — pursued women’s votes through constitutional means: petitions, meetings, lobbying MPs, and peaceful demonstration. Fawcett had been campaigning since the 1860s and believed patient constitutional pressure would succeed.

The suffragettes — the WSPU founded in 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst — took direct action: smashing windows, chaining themselves to railings, arson attacks on post boxes and empty buildings, and hunger strikes in prison. Emily Davison was killed at Epsom on 4 June 1913 when she ran onto the racecourse during the Derby. Emmeline’s daughters Christabel and Sylvia both played prominent roles, though they later disagreed: Christabel continued the militant campaign, while Sylvia worked with the labour movement and opposed the First World War.

Key Fact

Suffragists (NUWSS, led by Millicent Fawcett) used constitutional means — petitions and lobbying. Suffragettes (WSPU, led by Emmeline Pankhurst) used militant direct action — arson, window-smashing and hunger strikes. Examiners penalise using these terms interchangeably.

The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave the vote to all men over 21 and to women over 30 who met a property qualification. Around 8.4 million women gained the vote. The age and property bar on women was clearly discriminatory, but it prevented women — who outnumbered men after the war’s casualties — from forming a majority of the electorate.

Why 1918? Historians point to several factors: women’s vital contributions to the war effort (munitions, nursing, transport) made it impossible to deny their civic participation; the WSPU had suspended militancy during the war and thrown itself into patriotic service; the Representation of the People Act was also driven by the need to give the vote to millions of servicemen who had lost it by moving away from their homes. Full equal franchise came in 1928, when the Equal Franchise Act lowered the voting age for women to 21, equalising the franchise.
before.exam_tip_html: Examiner reports for this unit specifically flag the error of using “suffragette” as a generic term for all women who campaigned for the vote. The WSPU (Emmeline Pankhurst) and the NUWSS (Millicent Fawcett) were distinct organisations with different tactics and different views on the effectiveness of militancy. In an “Explain Why” question on why women won the vote in 1918, a top-band answer will weigh both organisations’ contributions alongside the impact of the First World War — and should not present the WSPU as the sole or even primary cause.

before.content_html:
The First World War and State Power

Before 1914, the British state was small by modern standards. The Liberal reforms of 1906–11 (old age pensions, national insurance) had begun building a social safety net, but most aspects of daily life were unregulated. The Defence of the Realm Act (DORA), passed just days after war was declared in August 1914, transformed this overnight. DORA allowed the government to requisition factories, control food supplies, censor newspapers, restrict pub opening hours and conscript men into the armed forces.

By 1918 the state had taken control of the railways, the coal mines, parts of the food supply chain, and vast quantities of private property. The total number of civil servants more than doubled during the war. When the war ended, some of this control was relaxed — but the experience had shown that a modern industrial state could, if it chose, direct the economy on a massive scale.

Key Fact

DORA (1914) gave the government powers to requisition factories and property, censor the press, control food supplies, restrict pub hours, and ultimately conscript men. It was the most extensive peacetime-to-wartime expansion of state power in British history to that point.

The Second World War and the Beveridge Report

The Second World War (1939–1945) repeated and deepened the pattern of state expansion. The Emergency Powers (Defence) Act (1939) gave Churchill’s wartime coalition even more sweeping powers than DORA had provided. Rationing, the direction of labour, and the evacuation of children all demonstrated the state’s capacity to organise civilian life. Women entered the workforce in unprecedented numbers — factory work, the Auxiliary Territorial Service, nursing, land work.

In 1942, the economist William Beveridge published his report “Social Insurance and Allied Services.” Beveridge identified five “Giant Evils” in British society: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness. He proposed a comprehensive welfare state that would protect every citizen “from the cradle to the grave.” The report sold 600,000 copies and was enormously popular, reflecting a wartime consensus that the sacrifices of ordinary people deserved a better post-war settlement.

In July 1945 the Labour Party under Clement Attlee won a landslide general election, defeating Winston Churchill despite (or perhaps because of) Churchill’s wartime leadership. Labour won 393 seats to the Conservatives’ 213. The result reflected a desire for social change: servicemen and their families wanted the post-war world to be different from the interwar years of mass unemployment and the Great Depression.

Attlee’s government (1945–51) implemented the Beveridge vision: the National Insurance Act (1946) created a welfare safety net for the unemployed, sick and elderly; the NHS was founded on 5 July 1948; the Education Act of 1944 (actually a wartime Conservative measure under R.A. Butler) had already established secondary education for all. The government also nationalised major industries: coal, railways, electricity, gas, steel and the Bank of England passed into public ownership.

The Post-War Consensus

The welfare state and the mixed economy created a post-war consensus: a broad agreement across the major parties that the state had a duty to maintain full employment, fund the NHS, and provide a social safety net. This consensus was not just Labour’s achievement. The 1944 Education Act was Conservative; the Beveridge Report was by a Liberal; Churchill had commissioned it. When the Conservatives returned to power under Winston Churchill in 1951, they did not dismantle the NHS or the nationalised industries — suggesting that the welfare settlement had wide public support.

The consensus began to fracture in the 1970s. Britain joined the EEC in 1973, raising questions about where sovereignty now lay. The “Winter of Discontent” (1978–79) — a period of widespread strikes by public sector workers — damaged the Labour government of James Callaghan and created the conditions for Margaret Thatcher’s election victory in 1979, which would challenge the post-war consensus directly.

Key Fact

The post-war consensus was the cross-party agreement (roughly 1945–1979) that the state should maintain full employment, public welfare, and key nationalised industries. The NHS (1948) and the National Insurance Act (1946) were its centrepieces under Attlee; the Conservatives kept both when they returned to power in 1951.

Britain’s entry into the EEC in January 1973 under Edward Heath’s Conservative government was controversial because EEC membership involved accepting Community law as superior to Acts of Parliament in areas of Community competence (trade, agriculture, competition). This raised fundamental questions about parliamentary sovereignty that had been central to British constitutional thinking since the seventeenth century. The conflict between Parliamentary sovereignty and EEC/EU law became one of the defining political debates of the following four decades.

A referendum on continued EEC membership was held in June 1975 under Harold Wilson’s Labour government; 67% voted to remain. The question of Britain’s relationship with European institutions, and what that meant for parliamentary sovereignty, remained unresolved and highly contested into the twenty-first century.
before.exam_tip_html: Impartiality note: when writing about the post-war welfare state, frame it as a cross-party achievement, not solely a Labour one. The 1942 Beveridge Report was by a Liberal economist; the 1944 Education Act was a Conservative measure; Churchill’s wartime coalition built the administrative framework. Presenting it as “what Labour achieved alone” misrepresents the historical record and reflects a political bias examiners can identify. Similarly, when discussing EEC entry in 1973, present both sides of the sovereignty argument factually — do not editorially endorse either Eurosceptic or pro-European positions.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways CND challenged government policy in the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. CND organised mass demonstrations attracting over 100,000 members when NATO stationed Cruise missiles in Western Europe — this created sustained political pressure on both parties; the Greenham Common Women's Peace Camp maintained a continuous presence outside the USAF base in Berkshire from 1981, generating international media coverage and keeping nuclear policy visible in public debate). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: vague reference to people protesting against nuclear weapons.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Miners' Strike of 1984-85 ended in defeat for the NUM.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (Thatcher's government had prepared for the confrontation — coal stocks were stockpiled and alternative fuels arranged, so the economic pressure of the strike was reduced; the NUM did not hold a national ballot before calling the strike, weakening its democratic legitimacy and preventing the TUC from calling general union support; violent confrontations such as Orgreave alienated public opinion; community division and family hardship among mining communities eventually broke solidarity). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes the strike without explaining why it failed.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Greenpeace was effective in challenging government and corporate decisions despite not holding political power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more factors with specific evidence (direct action tactics — occupying the Brent Spar platform and sailing ships into nuclear test zones — generated media coverage that made ignoring the issue politically costly; consumer pressure during the Brent Spar dispute led to a European boycott of Shell that changed the company's decision despite government support for deep-sea disposal; Greenpeace demonstrated that environmental concerns had broad public support, creating electoral incentives for government to act; high-profile campaigns shaped the political agenda on nuclear testing, whaling and eventually climate change). Secure: two factors with relevant evidence. Developing: describes Greenpeace campaigns accurately but does not explain the mechanism by which they were effective. Emerging: vague reference to public support.

practice_questions.text: How far did pressure groups in the period 1958-2007 successfully challenge the power of Parliament and government? [You may consider: CND; Greenpeace; the Miners' Strike; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument addressing both success and failure — success: Greenpeace Brent Spar victory; CND influenced Labour policy; mass protests (Iraq 2003 march) kept issues in public debate; failure: CND did not achieve nuclear disarmament; Miners' Strike ended in defeat; Blair ignored the 2003 Iraq march; Parliament and government retained ultimate decision-making power. Overall judgement about the extent of pressure group success and what kinds of pressure groups were more/less effective. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence from named groups; some imbalance. Developing: describes pressure group activities accurately but does not weigh success against failure. Emerging: narrative of events without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main features of Prime Ministerial power under Thatcher or Blair.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points about either Thatcher or Blair (or both with comparison) — Thatcher: centralised decision-making; sidelined dissenting cabinet ministers; confrontational approach to unions; removed by own MPs 1990 over poll tax and Europe; Blair: 179-seat majority 1997; 'sofa government' style; Iraq War 2003 against cabinet advice and mass public opposition; constitutional reforms — devolution, Human Rights Act. Secure: two or three relevant points with supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to these PMs having a lot of power.

before.content_html:
Pressure Groups and Democratic Participation

A pressure group is an organisation that campaigns on specific issues without seeking political power itself. By the late twentieth century, as public trust in political parties declined, pressure groups became increasingly important channels of democratic participation. The spec focuses on three: the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND), Greenpeace, and the labour movement’s role in the Miners’ Strike.

Note carefully: the spec names these three groups specifically for this period (roughly 1958 onwards). Examiner reports have flagged students who bring in pressure groups from the wrong time period or from outside the spec. Use only these named examples unless you are making a clearly contextual comparison.

Key Fact

The three spec-named pressure groups are: CND (Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, founded 1958 — nuclear weapons); Greenpeace (founded 1971 — environmental protection); and the NUM (National Union of Mineworkers, the trade union at the centre of the 1984–85 Miners’ Strike).

CND and the Nuclear Disarmament Movement

The CND was founded in 1958 against the backdrop of the Cold War arms race. Its early patron was the philosopher Bertrand Russell. CND organised the Aldermaston Marches — annual demonstrations from London to the Atomic Weapons Establishment at Aldermaston, Berkshire — which attracted tens of thousands of participants in the early 1960s.

CND’s influence peaked during periods of Cold War tension — the 1960s (Cuban Missile Crisis) and the early 1980s (NATO’s decision to station Cruise and Pershing missiles in Western Europe). In the early 1980s CND attracted over 100,000 members. The Greenham Common Women’s Peace Camp (from 1981) maintained a continuous presence outside the USAF base in Berkshire. Despite these mass campaigns, CND did not achieve its core objective: Britain kept its nuclear deterrent. The campaign did, however, maintain public debate about nuclear weapons policy and influenced the Labour Party’s adoption of unilateral disarmament as policy in 1983.

Greenpeace was founded in 1971 in Vancouver, Canada, in opposition to US nuclear weapons testing in Alaska. It became a global organisation known for high-profile direct action: sailing ships into nuclear test zones, physically blocking the dumping of nuclear waste at sea, and later campaigning against whaling, deforestation and climate change.

Greenpeace’s most significant British controversy was the 1995 Brent Spar affair, when the organisation occupied a disused Shell oil platform to prevent it being sunk in the North Atlantic. European consumers boycotted Shell petrol stations and Shell eventually abandoned the deep-sea disposal plan. The episode showed how a pressure group could use direct action and public mobilisation to change corporate behaviour, even when the government supported the original plan. It also demonstrated that Greenpeace could succeed without winning a parliamentary vote.

The Miners’ Strike 1984–85

The Miners’ Strike of 1984–85 was the most significant industrial conflict in twentieth-century Britain. When the National Coal Board announced closure plans for uneconomic pits, Arthur Scargill’s NUM called a national strike in March 1984 without holding a national ballot. Thatcher’s government had prepared for this confrontation: coal stocks were stockpiled, alternative fuels arranged, and police from across the country deployed to manage picket lines.

The strike lasted a year and was marked by violent confrontations at sites like Orgreave coking plant (June 1984). Divided communities, hardship among miners’ families, and the lack of a national ballot weakened the NUM’s position. The TUC did not call general support. By March 1985 the miners returned to work defeated. Thatcher went on to privatise many nationalised industries, breaking up the post-war consensus that the state should own key economic infrastructure.

Key Fact

The miners returned to work in March 1985 without achieving their objectives. The defeat broke the NUM’s power and was followed by privatisation of coal and other industries, ending the post-war consensus that the state should own strategic industries. It marked a decisive shift in the balance between trade unions and government.

The spec requires study of “Prime Ministerial power under Thatcher and Blair.” Both are significant cases of a Prime Minister operating with exceptional personal authority. Margaret Thatcher (Prime Minister 1979–1990) centralised decision-making in Downing Street, sidelining cabinet ministers who disagreed with her, and described herself as “the best man in the Cabinet.” Her style was openly confrontational — the Miners’ Strike was in part a deliberate decision to defeat the unions rather than negotiate. She was ultimately removed by her own MPs in November 1990 over the poll tax and European policy.

Tony Blair (Prime Minister 1997–2007) came to power with a 179-seat majority and also concentrated power in Downing Street, using a “sofa government” of informal advisers alongside formal cabinet structures. Critics argued that Blair’s decision to join the US invasion of Iraq in 2003 — despite a massive CND-linked protest march of over one million people in London in February 2003 — showed that Prime Ministerial power could override both cabinet and popular opinion in security matters.
before.exam_tip_html: For questions on pressure groups in this unit, only use CND, Greenpeace and the NUM unless the question specifically asks about pressure groups in general. Examiner reports have docked marks from students who brought in examples from outside the named period (e.g. the Chartists, the WSPU) or from beyond the spec’s named groups. When assessing effectiveness, make sure you explain the criterion — did CND achieve its stated goal (nuclear disarmament)? No. Did it influence public debate and Labour Party policy? Yes. Good analytical answers address what “success” means before judging it.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the devolution settlement established in Scotland in 1999.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific feature (e.g. the Scottish Parliament could pass primary legislation on devolved matters including health, education and justice) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. it also had tax-varying powers — the ability to raise or lower income tax by up to 3p in the pound, giving it greater fiscal autonomy than any previous devolved body). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to Scotland having its own parliament. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 2010 coalition government.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. the coalition was formed after the 2010 election produced a hung Parliament — no party had an overall majority, requiring Conservative and Liberal Democrat leaders David Cameron and Nick Clegg to negotiate a formal agreement to govern together; the coalition agreed to raise university tuition fees to £9,000, breaking a prominent Liberal Democrat manifesto pledge — this caused the Liberal Democrats to lose 49 of 57 seats in 2015). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: vague reference to coalition government.

practice_questions.text: Explain why devolution in 1999 was a significant change in where power lay in the United Kingdom.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (the Scottish Parliament had primary legislative powers over health, education and justice — areas that directly affected millions of citizens, meaning decisions that previously required Westminster approval were now taken in Edinburgh; the creation of devolved bodies challenged the traditional doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty by giving legislative power to regional institutions for the first time since the Act of Union 1707; the close Welsh result (50.3%) showed uneven support but Blair's government proceeded — Westminster decided how much power to devolve rather than the regions themselves, showing limits to the change). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes devolution without explaining why it was significant.

practice_questions.text: Explain why coalition government created challenges for democratic accountability.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more factors with specific evidence (neither party could implement its full manifesto — voters could not hold the government accountable for promises broken through compromise rather than political failure; the tuition fees example showed a specific manifesto promise (Liberal Democrat pledge to abolish fees) broken as a condition of coalition — the Liberal Democrats suffered massive electoral punishment in 2015 as a result; coalition agreements are negotiated after the election, not voted on — critics argued this gave unelected negotiators power to determine policy; voters choosing one party could end up being governed partly by another's programme). Secure: two factors with relevant evidence. Developing: describes the difficulties of coalition without explaining why they raised accountability problems. Emerging: vague reference to parties disagreeing.

practice_questions.text: How far did devolution and the events of 1997-2014 represent a fundamental change in where power lay in Britain? [You may consider: the 1997 referendums; the Scottish Parliament; the Good Friday Agreement; the 2014 referendum; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument addressing both the scale of change (Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly with genuine legislative powers; Good Friday Agreement — power-sharing in Northern Ireland; 2014 referendum showed 44.7% of Scots wanted independence, reflecting deep dissatisfaction with Westminster) and continuity (Westminster remained sovereign — it could repeal devolution Acts; the 2014 result preserved the Union; coalition government showed Parliament still functioned normally; English law and most taxation remained at Westminster). Overall judgement on whether 'fundamental change' is the right description. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes devolution accurately but does not weigh the extent of change. Emerging: narrative without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the key facts about the 2014 Scottish independence referendum.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific, accurate points (held on 18 September 2014; result was 55.3% No, 44.7% Yes; turnout was 84.6% — the highest in any UK election or referendum since universal suffrage; led by SNP's Alex Salmond (Yes) and Better Together campaign (No); Better Together included Labour, Conservative and Liberal Democrat politicians; Scotland remained in the United Kingdom). Secure: two or three relevant points with some supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to Scotland voting to stay in the UK.

before.content_html:
Why Devolution?

By the 1990s, Scotland and Wales had long-standing political identities distinct from England. The Scottish National Party (SNP) had grown steadily since the 1970s. Scotland had voted for a devolved assembly in a 1979 referendum but the result was invalidated by a rule requiring 40% of the total electorate to vote Yes. In Wales, a 1979 referendum rejected devolution outright. The issue remained unresolved for two decades.

Devolution returned to the agenda under Tony Blair’s Labour government. In September 1997 — just months after Labour’s landslide election victory — referendums were held in both Scotland and Wales. In Scotland, 74.3% voted Yes to a Parliament with tax-varying powers. In Wales, the result was 50.3% Yes — a majority of fewer than 7,000 votes out of 1.1 million cast. Both votes showed that devolution had genuine but uneven support.

Key Fact

In September 1997, Scotland voted 74.3% Yes to devolution (with a separate question on tax-varying powers); Wales voted 50.3% Yes — a majority of under 7,000 votes. Both Parliaments opened in 1999. Scotland gained primary legislative and limited tax-varying powers; Wales gained secondary legislative powers only (later expanded).

The Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly

The Scottish Parliament opened in May 1999 under First Minister Donald Dewar, with powers over health, education, justice and local government. It could vary income tax by up to 3p in the pound. The Welsh Assembly, later renamed the Senedd, had more limited powers initially — it could pass secondary legislation but not primary Acts in most areas. Over subsequent years, the Scotland Act 2012 and 2016 expanded Scottish powers significantly, and the Wales Act 2017 moved Wales towards a similar model.

Devolution was controversial. Unionists feared it would lead to the break-up of the United Kingdom. Supporters of devolution argued it made government more responsive to local needs and democratic in distant regions. The “West Lothian Question” — first posed in the 1970s — asked why Scottish MPs at Westminster could vote on English health or education matters when English MPs had no equivalent say over Scottish issues. It remained constitutionally unresolved.

In April 1998 the Good Friday Agreement ended three decades of conflict in Northern Ireland. It established a power-sharing executive in which unionist and nationalist parties governed together, a North-South Ministerial Council linking institutions in Northern Ireland and the Republic, and commitments to human rights and decommissioning of paramilitary weapons. Supported in a referendum by 71% of voters in Northern Ireland and 94% in the Republic, it was a significant extension of devolved governance and power-sharing.

The Agreement was the result of a long negotiation process, and its implementation was not straightforward — devolved government in Northern Ireland was suspended several times between 1999 and 2007 before a more stable arrangement was reached. It is significant in the context of this unit because it demonstrated that Westminster was willing to share power with regional institutions even in the most politically sensitive part of the United Kingdom.

The 2010 Coalition and Challenges of Coalition Government

The general election of May 2010 produced a hung Parliament — no party had an overall majority. The Conservatives, led by David Cameron, won 306 seats; Labour won 258; the Liberal Democrats won 57. After five days of negotiations, Cameron and Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg announced a formal coalition agreement, creating the first peacetime coalition government in Britain since 1945.

The coalition faced immediate challenges. The two parties had different priorities: the Conservatives wanted rapid deficit reduction; the Liberal Democrats had pledged to abolish student tuition fees. When the coalition raised fees to £9,000, the Liberal Democrat vote collapsed. Coalition governance required both parties to compromise — raising questions about whether voters could hold governments accountable when no manifesto was actually implemented. The Liberal Democrats lost 49 of their 57 seats in the 2015 election.

Key Fact

A hung Parliament occurs when no party wins an outright majority. The 2010 Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition was the first peacetime coalition since 1945. It struggled with conflicting manifesto promises — especially tuition fees — and raised questions about democratic accountability when compromise means neither partner implements its electoral programme.

On 18 September 2014 Scotland held a referendum on independence. The SNP, led by Alex Salmond, campaigned for a Yes vote; the “Better Together” campaign (led by Labour, Conservative and Liberal Democrat politicians) campaigned for No. The result was 55.3% No, 44.7% Yes — on a turnout of 84.6%, the highest recorded in any UK election or referendum since universal suffrage.

These are the facts as recorded. The debate about Scottish independence involves deeply contested questions of national identity, economic viability, constitutional principle and democratic self-determination — questions on which this lesson takes no view. Presenting the referendum result and its context is not an endorsement of either position. The high turnout suggests that questions about where power should lie — the central theme of this 1,000-year unit — remained intensely relevant to people in 2014.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1997 devolution referendums led to the Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly opening in 1999 — the most significant change to the UK's constitutional structure since Irish independence in 1922.
  • The 2010 Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition was the first peacetime coalition since 1945 and raised fundamental questions about democratic accountability when two parties govern on a compromise programme neither campaigned for.
  • The 2014 Scottish independence referendum (55.3% No, on 84.6% turnout) showed that questions about where power lies remained intensely politically alive at the end of this unit’s thousand-year sweep.
before.exam_tip_html: For questions on devolution and the 2014 referendum, examiners expect factual precision and political neutrality. State the referendum result figures accurately (Scotland 1997: 74.3% Yes; Wales 1997: 50.3% Yes; Scotland 2014: 55.3% No, 44.7% Yes). Do not editorially endorse either side of the independence question — your job is to explain why it happened and what it shows about where power lies in Britain, not to argue a political case. In “Change and Continuity” essays, devolution is a strong example of how parliamentary sovereignty was modified in the late twentieth century — but note that Westminster retained the power to grant or withhold devolved powers.
